extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in composing or evaluating epic/heroic poetry (e.g., Milton's Paradise Lost)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging epic/heroic poetry, especially on description, character-speech, poetic 'machines' (plot devices), classical allusion, and tonal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lavish ornamentation on weak/unactive parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet has observed Aristotle's Rule of lavishing all the Ornaments of Diction on the weak unactive Parts of the Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As noted in the footnote quoting Aristotle: 'The diction should be most laboured in the idle parts of the poem; those in which neither manners nor sentiments prevail; for the manners and the sentiments are only obscured by too splendid a diction.' In practice, concentrate florid, elaborate expressions in descriptive/idle passages where sentiment and character do not already supply beauty; avoid over-labouring parts where manners and sentiments dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify length of natural description by dramatic necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Drawings of Gardens, Rivers, Rainbows, and the like dead Pieces of Nature, are justly censured in an Heroic Poem, when they run out into an unnecessary length; the Description of Paradise would have been faulty, had not the Poet been very particular in it, not only as it is the Scene of the Principal Action, but as it is requisite to give us an Idea of that Happiness from which our first Parents fell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lengthy descriptive passages are defensible only when they serve the scene, character, or thematic stakes (e.g., to establish the pre-fall happiness). Otherwise they risk being irrelevant and weakening the heroic poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions should establish thematic stakes (pre-fall happiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description of Paradise is requisite to give us an Idea of that Happiness from which our first Parents fell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use description to make the reader grasp what is lost or at stake; descriptions should illuminate the poem's central themes and justify the poem's moral/emotional contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting's influence on character thought and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: As the Criticks have remarked, that in those Poems, wherein Shepherds are Actors, the Thoughts ought always to take a Tincture from the Woods, Fields and Rivers, so we may observe, that our first Parents seldom lose Sight of their happy Station in any thing they speak or do; ... their Thoughts are always Paradisiacal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters' language, imagery, and concerns should be consistently colored by their environment; maintain this integration to reinforce verisimilitude and thematic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artful raising and ordering of conflicting passions
rubrics_metrics.description: This Conflict of Passions is raised with a great deal of Art, as the opening of his Speech to the Sun is very bold and noble. Satan ... reflects upon the happy Condition from which he fell, and breaks forth into a Speech that is softned with several transient Touches of Remorse and Self-accusation: But at length he confirms himself in Impenitence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray complex emotional shifts within a speech or scene with careful art so the progression (remorse → reaffirmation of evil, etc.) reads natural, rhetorically powerful, and character-consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot 'machines' (devices) should surprise yet be artfully connected
rubrics_metrics.description: His bounding over the Walls of Paradise; his sitting in the Shape of a Cormorant upon the Tree of Life ... his transforming himself into different Shapes, in order to hear their Conversation, are Circumstances that give an agreeable Surprize to the Reader, and are devised with great Art, to connect that Series of Adventures in which the Poet has engaged this Artificer of Fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metamorphoses, covert approaches, and other devices to create surprise but ensure they are plausibly integrated into the narrative arc and sustain the chain of adventures; avoid gratuitous tricks that don't advance the fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasteful use of classical borrowings and analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton is every where full of Hints and sometimes literal Translations, taken from the greatest of the Greek and Latin Poets. ... The breaking off the Combat between Gabriel and Satan, by the hanging out of the Golden Scales in Heaven, is a Refinement upon Homers Thought ... Milton ... makes an artful use of it for the proper carrying on of his Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow classical images or scenes when they illuminate or advance the poem's action; classical allusion is justified especially when adapted to serve dramatic purposes rather than as mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic embellishments must serve dramatic function
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton ... does not only insert it as a Poetical Embellishment, like the Authors above-mentioned; but makes an artful use of it for the proper carrying on of his Fable, and for the breaking off the Combat between the two Warriors, who were upon the point of engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that striking poetic devices (allegories, scale-weighings, omens) have an operative role in the plot or in controlling pacing/scene breaks, rather than being purely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petty prettiness beneath a great poet's genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Uriel's gliding down to the Earth upon a Sunbeam, with the Poets Device to make him descend ... is a Prettiness that might have been admired in a little fanciful Poet, but seems below the Genius of Milton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a tonal register commensurate with the poem's stature; avoid small, cute conceits or gimmicks that jar with the elevated tone of a great epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity and epic grandeur in imagery and simile
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan cloathing himself with Terror when he prepares for the Combat is truly sublime, and at least equal to Homers Description of Discord ... or to that of Fame in Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for the sublime, employ bold, concentrated imagery and comparisons worthy of classical exemplars; such images should elevate the scene to epic scale and match the poem's ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speeches must conform to character (moral and temperamental consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: His Answer upon his being discovered, and demanded to give an Account of himself, is conformable to the Pride and Intrepidity of his Character. The Conference between Gabriel and Satan abounds with Sentiments proper for the Occasion, and suitable to the Persons of the two Speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each speech's diction, tone, and argumentative moves are consistent with the speaker's established traits and moral makeup; appropriateness to occasion and person is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain dignity, modesty, and naturalness in tender/innocent scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: They are the Gallantries of Paradise ... The Professions they make to one another are full of Warmth: but at the same time founded on Truth. ... to have made the Man speak the most endearing things, without descending from his natural Dignity, and the Woman receiving them without departing from the Modesty of her Character; in a Word, to adjust the Prerogatives of Wisdom and Beauty, and make each appear to the other in its proper Force and Loveliness. This mutual Subordination of the two Sexes is wonderfully kept up in the whole Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tender or erotic passages in a state of innocence should avoid artifice and hyperbole; preserve the man's dignity and the woman's modesty, balance mutual esteem, and make affection feel truthful rather than exaggerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft tender parts so as to please delicate readers without offending the severe
rubrics_metrics.description: These Passages are all worked off with so much Art, that they are capable of pleasing the most delicate Reader, without offending the most severe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose delicate scenes with refined judgment so they are emotionally resonant and tasteful to sensitive readers while standing up to strict critical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit speech-attribution (he said) only with judgment to preserve naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the Modern Heroick Poets have imitated the Ancients, in beginning a Speech without premising, that the Person said thus or thus; but ... it requires Judgment to do it in such a manner as they shall not be missed, and that the Speech may begin naturally without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you begin a speech without an introductory tag, ensure the opening is so natural and clear that readers are not disoriented; the omission should enhance, not hinder, readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masterly transitions between modes and scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall close my Reflections upon this Book, with observing the Masterly Transition which the Poet makes to their Evening Worship in the following Lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitions (e.g., from narrative action to worship or from day to evening scenes) should be handled skillfully to preserve flow and to shift tone without jarring the reader.
